newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Utilicorp loosens grip on councils' Power stake.
newsitem.headline: Utilicorp loosens grip on councils' Power stake.

text.p: Utilicorp New Zealand has agreed to remove one of the legal impediments to Power New Zealand's council shareholders selling to its rival, Mercury Energy, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Monday.

In so doing it has reduced the legal risk the councils face if they accept Mercury's offer of $10 a share, or $108 million in total, instead of the substantially lower offer on the table from Utilicorp.
How much lower became clear this week when Utilicorp filed with the stock exchange details of its offer, which becomes effective on November 19.
The Thames-Coromandel, Matamata-Piako, South Waikato and Hauraki district councils own 7.1 percent of Power New Zealand.
Mercury has 33 percent, while Utilicorp owns 30 percent outright and has an interest in a further 8 percent held by its associate, WEL Energy.
Utilicorp is offering the councils $8 a share, increasing by 8.2 percent a year for up to three years. However, any dividends paid by Power New Zealand would be deducted from the price.
And Utilicorp's money would not be available up front. The councils can sell up to half their shares in August 1998 and the balance not until March 2000.
Nevertheless, the councils seem set to spurn the bird in the hand for 80 percent of a bird in the bush.

A briefing paper prepared by the councils' general managers last month said that Utilicorp had made it clear it was not prepared to match Mercury's $10 offer. It believed the shares to be encumbered and this justified the discount.
On July 24, Utilicorp and the councils agreed orally to enter into a shareholders' agreement in return for the United States company making an offer of $7.25 for the councils' shares.

Mercury contends that this agreement breached the takeovers rules that Power New Zealand shareholders had just adopted, which require Utilicorp as an insider to give 15 days' public notice of any such transaction.
Utilicorp disputes this but at the councils' request has unconditionally cancelled and withdrawn the oral undertaking.
That undertaking was cited in the general managers' briefing paper. "There is a higher legal risk in transacting with Mercury, given the commitments as they exist at this time," they said.
"This risk reduces if Utilicorp withdraws the undertakings provided in the transcript of July 24."
But the July agreement is only part of the legal barbed wire in which the councils find themselves entangled.
Technically, they do not own the PNZ shares directly; they have been transferred, for tax reasons, into special purpose holding companies (Lates).
The councils' lawyers, Chapman Tripp, have advised them that the controversial standstill agreement entered into by the councils when they were allotted the shares in 1994 do not apply to the Lates.

Power New Zealand only agreed to the transfer of shares from the councils to the Lates after the councils in July gave it an undertaking that they would enter into a shareholders' agreement with Utilicorp. So far this has not happened.
"We are advised that this, whilst enforceable, may well be a breach of the stock exchange listing rules," the general managers said.
However, Power New Zealand might accept delisting as the lesser evil Compared with a sale to Mercury, they said.
Utilicorp has a "golden share" in each of the Lates, which effectively allows it to veto the Late from selling its PNZ shares to Mercury.
Any sale to Mercury would therefore have to be by means of the council selling its shares in the Late.
